archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A team controlling play at 5-on-5 as well as anyone in the league, held to .500 by sub-replacement goaltending, a poor penalty kill and cold finishing that should not last.

report.headline: Best shot share in the league, buried by goaltending and a leaky kill
report.take:
New Jersey is 3-3-0, sits sixth in the Metropolitan and 19th on the site's Teams tab, with a differential of -6 that ranks 23rd per game. Those numbers describe a mediocre team. The 5-on-5 numbers describe something else: an xGF % of 60.3 and a CF % of 62, both first in the league. The Devils have the puck, they are generating the better chances, and so far they have very little to show for it.

The gap between process and results comes down to two things. The first is in net. Goalies GSAx sits at -3.7 (24th) and the goaltending grade is a D+. Jake Allen has been roughly average-adjacent at .885 over four starts, while Nico Daws' two starts produced an .824 and -3.3 GSAx on his own, which accounts for most of the hole. The second is the penalty kill at 70.6%, 27th in the league. Add cold shooting and you get a PDO of 93.6, which is extreme and almost never holds. The defense allowing the most points in the league to opposing centers and defensemen fits that pattern: a team giving up few chances but having the ones it does allow, plus power-play goals, go in.

What the numbers hide is that the record is, if anything, slightly flattering relative to the goal margin. Pts vs Goal Diff is +1.2 (7th), courtesy of one-goal wins over Philadelphia and Detroit offsetting a 6-0 loss on Long Island. So the turnaround has to come from the underlying play converting, not from close-game luck evening out. Up front the work is concentrated: Jack Hughes (8 points, 68.2% xGF) and Jesper Bratt (7 points, 70% xGF) are driving it, while Timo Meier has no goals on 25 shots and Dawson Mercer none on 15. The shot volume is real; the finishing is due.

Context matters before declaring a new identity. Last season the Devils posted a 49.5% xGF with the 27th-ranked offense, and even the strong 2022-23 club sat at 56%. Sixty percent over a handful of games will come down. But a team that sustains even a mid-50s share with league-average goaltending is a playoff team, and that is the more likely direction than the standings suggest.

strengths.title: League-best 5-on-5 control
strengths.body: The Devils lead the league in both xGF % and CF %, and every regular skater listed is above 53% xGF. That breadth matters: it is not one line padding the numbers but the whole lineup tilting the ice. The level will regress toward last season's middling share, but this is the most predictive part of the profile.

strengths.title: Hughes and Bratt driving the top
strengths.body: Jack Hughes, at 21.5 minutes a night, and Bratt are producing at a high clip with dominant on-ice chance shares, and both rank near the top of their position tabs. They also anchor a power play converting at 23.8%, seventh in the league. With this kind of possession behind them, their production looks sustainable.

strengths.title: Shooting luck owed back
strengths.body: A PDO of 93.6 is far below the 100 average and reflects both poor team save percentage and cold shooting. Meier's zero goals on 25 shots is the poster case. Few teams stay this far below average for long, so goals for should rise even if the shot share settles.

concerns.title: Goaltending is costing games
concerns.body: The tandem is 24th in GSAx, and Daws' .824 in two starts is the main drag. Allen's numbers are closer to playable but not good enough to steal anything. History cuts both ways: the 2024-25 group saved 23.3 goals above expected, but 2023-24 and last season were negative, so a correction to average is plausible, not guaranteed.

concerns.title: Penalty kill near the bottom
concerns.body: A 70.6% kill ranks 27th and turns the Devils' even-strength edge into a wash on nights they take penalties. Part of it is goaltending, since a kill lives on its goalie's save percentage. The franchise has run kills around 80% or better for years, so this should improve, but it is the most dangerous weakness against power-play teams.

concerns.title: Points leaking to centers and defensemen
concerns.body: Opponents' centers and defensemen are scoring well above their own averages against New Jersey, both ranked last in the league. Defensemen taking a far bigger share of the points against than the league norm hints at point shots and power-play looks getting through. With a strong shot share this reads more as save-percentage noise than structural failure, but it bears watching.

trend.note: The Devils have alternated results all month, never winning two straight and dropping two in a row once, with the scorelines swinging from a 6-0 loss to a 4-1 win. The underlying play has been steadier than the results.

weekAhead.headline: Three home games, an elite Rangers goalie and Anaheim's power play
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the Rangers at home, a 6-2-0 division leader third on the site, and it is the cleanest test of New Jersey's model. The Rangers have been out-attempted at 5-on-5 (46% CF) and sit at a 50.6% xGF, but their goaltending leads the league in GSAx and their PDO is 105.4. Expect the Devils to carry play; whether it shows on the scoreboard depends on solving a hot goalie. Washington on the road is a .500 team with a D+ forward group and a 13.3% power play, the softest matchup of the week for a shaky kill.

Colorado comes in with the league's top offense and the same D+ goaltending grade as New Jersey, which sets up a potentially high-event game where the Devils' possession edge should translate into chances against a vulnerable net. Anaheim closes the week with a 33.3% power play, third in the league, but a 47.4% xGF; win at 5-on-5 and stay out of the box is the entire game plan. Three of four at home and a likely possession edge in every game make a winning week realistic, but the goaltending has to hold up.

keyMatchups.title: Devils' shots vs Rangers' goaltending
keyMatchups.body: New York's goalies lead the league in GSAx and its defense ranks second in goals against, despite a negative shot share. That is the mirror image of New Jersey: process versus finishing. One game won't settle it, but it is a direct test of whether the Devils' chances can beat a hot goalie.

keyMatchups.title: Avalanche firepower meets shaky nets
keyMatchups.body: Colorado leads the league in scoring but its goalies are 26th in GSAx, and its defense lets opposing defensemen score above their averages. Luke Hughes and Dougie Hamilton, who lead the Devils' blue line in shots, should get looks. Expect goals at both ends.

keyMatchups.title: Ducks power play vs Devils' kill
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim converts a third of its power plays while New Jersey kills barely seven in ten. The Ducks are out-chanced at 5-on-5, so special teams are their clearest route to an upset. Discipline decides this one.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net and what the team save percentage looks like; if Allen or Daws posts league-average numbers, the shot share should finally show up in the standings.

restOfSeason.body:
The 60%-plus shot and chance shares will not hold; expect them to drift back toward the low-to-mid 50s, where this core has usually lived. But the PDO of 93.6 and the 70.6% kill are further from normal and should rebound harder, which nets out in New Jersey's favor. Hughes, Bratt and Hischier give the forward group enough finishing at the top, and Meier and Mercer should start converting their volume.

The real variable is goaltending. If Allen settles near average and the second goalie stops hemorrhaging, this profile fits a playoff team in a division where Carolina and the Rangers have broken out early. If the GSAx keeps sinking, the Devils could repeat last season's pattern of good-enough play and a middling finish. The +1.2 Pts vs Goal Diff means they have not yet been unlucky in close games, so the improvement has to come from the margin itself.

confidence.note: Six games; shot shares stabilize faster than save percentage, but everything here is early.
